candidates.title: Direct Rapid Recharge Controls the Hydrological Response in a Peri‐Urban Mountainous Tropical Catchment
candidates.authors: Mena‐Rivera, Leonardo; Esquivel‐Hernández, Germain; Villalobos‐Forbes, Mario; Sánchez‐Gutiérrez, Rolando; Sánchez‐Murillo, Ricardo; Castro‐Chacón, Laura …
candidates._abstract: ABSTRACT In the wet tropics, the seasonal changes in rainfall amounts are altering catchment storage and, consequently, groundwater‐to‐surface water connectivity. However, estimations of water source contributions to streamflow remain poorly constrained across mountainous headwater catchments. Here, we use stable isotopes (δ 18 O and δ 2 H), 222 Rn activity and electrical conductivity (EC) to characterise the hydrological responses in the northern mountainous region of the Central Valley, Costa Rica. Temporal trends revealed a clear response in groundwater–surface water connectivity to rainfall inputs. Streamflow transitioned from being dominated mainly by groundwater during the dry season to a greater contribution of subsurface flow during the wet season. We found that direct rapid recharge regulates this hydrological connectivity during the rainiest periods, as demonstrated by increased 222 Rn activity in both springs and streams. Using a mass balance approach, we estimated monthly groundwater contributions to streamflow using 222 Rn activity (5.9%–63.1%) and EC (37.2%–84.0%). A Bayesian endmember mixing model yielded similar mean groundwater contributions compared to the mass balance approach depending on tracer selection (EC– 222 Rn: 56.2% ± 12.7%, δ 18 O– 222 Rn: 51.1% ± 11.6% and δ 18 O–EC: 89.2% ± 5.2%). Our findings are useful for future assessments of the impact of climate change in rainfall amount and seasonality on groundwater recharge and streamflow generation in tropical mountainous catchments.

candidates.title: Organic Matter Dynamics and Biogeochemical Signatures in Lakes From the Prairies to Tundra in Western Canada
candidates.authors: Préskienis, Vilmantas; Kivilä, E. Henriikka; Bogard, Matthew J.; Cheecham-Uhrich, Dënë; Blais, Jules M.; Rautio, Milla
candidates._abstract: Abstract Climate‐driven poleward shifts of terrestrial ecosystems are expected to alter organic matter inputs and biogeochemical processes in northern lakes. In regions lacking long‐term observations, latitudinal gradients provide valuable space‐for‐time substitutions for predicting these changes. We sampled water columns and sediments from 23 lakes across six ecoregions spanning the Canadian Prairies, boreal forest, and tundra to identify spatial patterns in organic matter composition, carbon burial, and dissolved greenhouse gases (GHG; notably CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O). Catchment characteristics strongly influenced lake biogeochemistry by regulating terrestrial organic matter inputs and water column mixing. Lakes along the southern treeline exhibited the highest sediment GHG concentrations, co‐occurring with abundant labile allochthonous organic matter, long warm summers, and conditions favoring thermal stratification. In contrast, exposed Prairie and tundra lakes remained well‐mixed and displayed similar biogeochemical characteristics despite contrasting climates. We further noticed increased algal (particularly cyanobacterial) and methanogenic production in lakes with catchments recently affected by extensive wildfires, suggesting that wildfires may further amplify climate‐driven changes in northern lake ecosystems. Our findings highlight the strong coupling between terrestrial ecosystems and freshwater biogeochemistry, improving our ability to predict how lake carbon cycling may respond to future northward shifts of terrestrial ecosystems.

candidates.title: Leakage from Traditional Irrigation Systems and Groundwater Upwelling Buffer the Impact of Heavy Streamflow Diversion on Benthic Biodiversity
candidates.authors: Casas, J. Jesús; Fenoy, Encarnación; Rubio, J. L.; Villegas, Jorge; Salinas-Bonillo, Maria Jacoba; Zakaluk, Thomas …
candidates._abstract: Headwater streams are biodiversity-rich yet highly vulnerable ecosystems, especially in Mediterranean mountain regions where hydrological regimes are increasingly altered by irrigation and climate change. We assessed the effects of flow reduction by traditional irrigation weirs on benthic macroinvertebrate communities in five headwaters within the National–Natural Park of Sierra Nevada. We sampled upstream (reference) and downstream (flow-impacted) sites of the weirs in spring and autumn. We also quantified stream physicochemical characteristics and macroinvertebrates, and evaluated changes in their community structure. Flow reduction downstream of the abstraction points was severe (76–98% of discharge in upstream reaches), yet downstream reaches remained without significant water chemical alteration, and flow — although minimal — was perennial through the year due to seepage from ditches and upwelling groundwater. Macroinvertebrate density was substantially reduced downstream, particularly in spring (≈ 50% lower). While local (α) and interlocal (β) diversities and community composition did not differ significantly between reach types, flow reduction consistently impaired regional (γ) diversity. Moreover, taxa richness of collectors and several biotic indices — based on Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera — significantly decreased in flow-impacted sites. These findings support incorporating EPT-based metrics to enhance the sensitivity of ecological quality assessments in mountain rivers. Overall, maintaining hydrological connectivity through leaky traditional irrigation systems appears pivotal for mitigating further losses of local biodiversity, particularly in impacted reaches that lack groundwater inflow. Furthermore, since even moderate local diversity losses can accumulate to reduce regional diversity, preserving as many stream reaches as possible with natural, or modified flow compatible with biodiversity conservation, is mandatory, particularly in biodiversity hotspots.

candidates.title: Potentially Toxic Elements in Surface Sediments of Black-Necked Crane Habitats: A Case Study of Plateau Lakes in Shangri-La, Yunnan, China
candidates.authors: Li, Mumo; Peng, Zhen; He, Zhenghua; Liu, Shilong; Li, Xu; Yang, Hua …
candidates._abstract: Plateau wetlands provide important wintering habitats for migratory waterbirds, making the assessment of environmental contamination relevant to their conservation. Characterizing potentially toxic elements in lake sediments provides a basis for identifying contamination patterns and prioritizing environmental monitoring in these habitats. Here, we assessed potentially toxic element contamination in surface sediments and potential ecological risks in three plateau lakes supporting wintering black-necked cranes (Grus nigricollis) in Shangri-La, Yunnan, China. In January 2025, 131 composite sediment samples (0–20 cm) were collected from Bitahai, Shudu, and Napahai lakes. Concentrations of Cu, Zn, Pb, As, Hg, and Cd were determined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Contamination and potential ecological risks were evaluated using the geo-accumulation index (Igeo) and potential ecological risk index (PERI), respectively. Potential sources were investigated using EPA PMF 5.0. Sediments were generally unpolluted to slightly polluted. Mean PERI values were 65.2, 62.7, and 76.5, respectively, indicating low potential ecological risk, with Cd and Hg contributing most. PMF resolved four factors tentatively associated with traffic/domestic emissions, agricultural/combustion inputs, localized inputs, and natural/regional sources. These findings provide a baseline for sediment monitoring and environmental management of black-necked crane wintering habitats, with particular attention to Cd, Hg, and As.

candidates.title: Alteration of Mineral Balances in Groundwater and Surface Waters of Mangalmé: Correlation Matrix and Heterogeneous Critical Anomaliese
candidates.authors: Mahamat, Hassan; Adannou, Haroun Ali; Yaya, Yaya; Adam, Balkis; Mohammed, Mohagir Ahmed; Belal, Mohammedain
candidates._abstract: This study focuses on a semi-arid area of Chad—the Mangalmé department—where access to drinking water remains a major concern. The population relies primarily on groundwater (wells) and surface water (ponds/reservoirs) for drinking and domestic use. These resources are affected by climate change, notably through declining water table levels, the disappearance of water bodies, drought, and the degradation of vegetation cover. Compounding these issues are anthropogenic pressures linked to agriculture, livestock farming, and sanitation. The aim of this study is to assess the physicochemical quality of these waters, identify critical anomalies, and determine the sources of contamination in order to provide data useful for health and environmental management. To this end, ten (10) localities were monitored over a three-month period (March, April, and May). Water samples from wells and ponds were collected, georeferenced using GPS, stored in cool boxes, and analyzed in the laboratory. In situ measurements included pH at 25°C, electrical conductivity, total dissolved solids, and turbidity. Chemical analyses covered total hardness (CaCO 3 ), calcium (Ca 2 + ), magnesium (Mg 2 + ), potassium (K + ), sodium (Na + ), bicarbonates (HCO 3 − ), chlorides (Cl − ), sulfates (SO 4 2 − ), nitrates (NO 3 − ), fluorides (F − ), iron (Fe), and ammonium (NH 4 + ). The methods employed included volumetry, flame photometry, and HACH 2800 spectrophotometry. A correlation matrix and a normalized multiparameter comparison were used to interpret the relationships between parameters. The results reveal heterogeneous mineralization. Some water sources exhibit high conductivity and dissolved solids, very high turbidity, iron and fluoride concentrations exceeding WHO guidelines, and alarming ammonium levels. pH values vary, reflecting distinct geological and anthropogenic conditions. The correlation matrix reveals a strong interdependence among conductivity, dissolved solids, calcium, magnesium, chlorides, and sulfates, suggesting a common origin or similar chemical interactions. In conclusion, none of the ten sources analyzed fully meet potability criteria without treatment. The contamination is twofold: natural—linked to the weathering of sedimentary rocks (sandstone, carbonates, fluorite) that release fluoride and iron—and anthropogenic, involving ammonium from domestic, agricultural, and livestock waste. These findings necessitate regular monitoring, appropriate treatment, and measures to protect water resources.

candidates.title: Poor taste in Texas: Tracing dissolved solid origins across the relict margin of the Greater Permian Evaporite Basin, Wichita River Watershed, north-central Texas, USA
candidates.authors: Miller, Nathan R.; Leybourne, Matthew I.
candidates._abstract: The greater Red River system of Texas and Oklahoma, USA, is historically underutilized due to high concentrations of dissolved solids (i.e., Na+, Cl−, SO42−). Catchment geology consists largely of N-striking Permian units that transition downstream from younger, highly soluble marine carbonates and evaporites to older, less soluble terrestrial siliciclastic units. Because Permian marine evaporite-bearing units have distinct Sr and S isotopic compositions, these constituents may effectively trace stratigraphic origins and downstream mixing behavior of the dissolved solid load. This hypothesis was tested for the Wichita River Watershed, an important sub-watershed of the upper Red River Basin. Major ions and stable isotopes (C, H, O, S, Sr) prove to be effective solute tracers in this system because of compositional contrasts between evaporite, carbonate, and silicate lithologic endmembers and the large 87Sr/86Sr range between Permian seawater (<0.707) and continental siliciclastic rocks (>0.710). Western headwaters are close to isotopic equilibrium with outcropping Blaine Formation gypsum, which prospectively correlates with San Andres Formation evaporites in the Permian basin based on comparable 87Sr/86Sr and δ34SSO4 values. Progressive downstream interaction with more radiogenic siliciclastic watershed units increases the dissolved solute 87Sr/86Sr signal to values approaching modern seawater (0.709) above its confluence with the Red River. Sulfur isotopes confirm a persistent Permian evaporite influence over sedimentary pyrite oxidation. These signatures contrast markedly from stream segments whose headwaters do not intersect evaporites. Study results demonstrate the efficacy of Permian evaporite geochemical tracers to characterize spatial variations in the dissolved solid load that directly impact water quality in watersheds intersecting Permian evaporite basins.

candidates.title: Linkages Between Dissolved Organic Matter Quality and Denitrification Potential in Surface Water and Groundwater Mixing Zones
candidates.authors: Wen, Zhang; Wang, Kaihang; Xue, Ping; Xian, Yang
candidates._abstract: ABSTRACT Nitrate contamination in surface water (SW) and groundwater (GW) represents a pervasive environmental challenge worldwide. The river‐riparian‐aquifer transition zone exerts a pivotal role in mediating nitrate export, primarily through promoting denitrification fueled by organic matter. In lowland riverine reaches, how compositional characteristics of organic matter regulate denitrification rates remains poorly elucidated, particularly in lowland reaches where processes are complicated by the combined effects of SW‐GW mixing, and heterogeneous environmental conditions. This study conducted field sampling of water and sediment across the riparian continuum (SW, SW‐GW mixing zone, and GW) along a representative lowland reach of the Han River. Denitrification potentials were quantified using the acetylene block technique, while the compositions and optical properties of organic matter were characterized via spectroscopic analyses. Partial least squares regression (PLSR; R 2 = 0.95) revealed that DOM quality dominates denitrification potential, with denitrifiers preferentially utilizing labile, microbially derived DOC components (C2), followed by terrestrial humic‐like components (C4) derived from riverbank sediments. During low‐flow periods, when labile protein‐like DOM was less available, SW‐GW mixing (river fraction of 10%–90%) was associated with enhanced utilization of sediment‐derived humic‐like C4 ( p < 0.05). This pattern is consistent with a priming‐like substrate‐switching mechanism, whereby small inputs of labile DOM and dynamic hydrological mixing stimulate the microbial use of semi‐labile sediment‐derived DOM. Such a mechanism helps sustain high denitrification potential in the mixing zone, highlighting the need to consider not only DOM quantity and quality, but also hydrologically mediated sediment OM processing in shallow riparian aquifers.

candidates.title: Hydrogeochemical controls on drinking and irrigation water suitability of spring water in the Champawat District, Uttarakhand: insights from multivariate statistical analysis
candidates.authors: Saxena, Aseem; Bahukhandi, Kanchan Deoli; Mahapatra, Durga Madhab; Tripathi, Sachin; Kumar, Manish
candidates._abstract: ABSTRACT In the Himalayan region of Uttarakhand, natural springs constitute the primary freshwater source for a large rural population. To investigate the spring water quality of the Lohawati catchment, 27 spring water samples (n = 27) were collected and analyzed to identify the contributions of geogenic and anthropogenic inputs to drinking and irrigation water quality. Major ions were found within the permissible limits, but fluoride exceeded 1 mg L−1, indicating potential fluorosis risk. The dominant hydrochemical facies are Ca2+–Mg2+–Cl−–SO42− and mixed types, with evapotranspiration and rock–water interaction as the primary processes controlling chemistry. Among heavy metals, Fe exceeded the acceptable limit (0.3 mg L−1), while Cu surpassed the permissible limit (0.05 mg L−1) in 66.7% of samples. Due to this metal load, the water quality index indicates that all samples fall into the ‘unsuitable for drinking’ category, yet they remain suitable for irrigation purposes. Correlation matrix and hierarchical cluster analyses suggest that elevated NO3- and SO42- concentrations are primarily associated with anthropogenic activities, particularly the use of fertilizers. Principal component analysis revealed that spring water quality is governed by the combined influence of geogenic and anthropogenic factors.

candidates.title: Microplastics in freshwater environments across the high altitude region of Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan
candidates.authors: Pittura, Lucia; Vita, Serafina; Resente, Mattia; Mongera, Federica; Khan, Adnan; Nafees, Maisoor Ahmed …
candidates._abstract: Microplastics are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in remote mountain freshwater ecosystems, yet evidence from high-altitude regions remains limited. This study investigated microplastics occurrence and characteristics in surface water, sediments, and fish from the Braldu-Shigar-Skardu freshwater system in Gilgit-Baltistan, northern Pakistan. Samples were collected from remote headwaters, tributaries, main river channels, and the Satpara Lake-Dam system. Fish originated from wild populations, farming facilities, and local markets to provide a broader assessment of microplastic exposure. Matrix-specific extraction protocols were applied, followed by stereomicroscope sorting and polymer identification by µFT-IR spectroscopy. Microplastics were detected in nearly all sites and matrices, with concentrations ranging from 1 to 17 MPs L -1 in water, 55–537 MPs kg -1 in sediments, and 1–11 MPs individual -1 in fish gastrointestinal tracts. Notably, highest frequency of microplastics occurrence was measured in farmed individuals (78%–83%), suggesting that aquaculture-related practices may represent an additional source of microplastics. Wild fish showed the lowest occurrence (25%), whereas those obtained from local markets revealed intermediate values (62%), indicating variable exposure across different pathways. Surface waters were dominated by small fragments and polypropylene, indicative of recent inputs and origin from fragmentation. Sediments showed a broader size distribution, and greater polymer diversity, consistent with their role as long-term sinks. The highest polymer diversity was highlighted in fish, indicating multiple exposure pathways. Spatial patterns did not show a geographical downstream increase, but rather a patchy distribution shaped by local anthropogenic input, hydrological connectivity, and depositional dynamics. Glacier-fed rivers primarily act as transport corridors, whereas low-energy environments such as Satpara Lake function as sinks promoting microplastics accumulation. Overall, the study provides the first integrated multi-compartment baseline for microplastics in Gilgit-Baltistan and supports future monitoring and management actions for these high altitude critical freshwater resources.

candidates.title: Unravelling the Natural and Anthropogenic Controls on Karst Groundwater Hydrochemistry in the Zaozhuang Area, Northern China: A Combined Hydrogeochemical and PMF Source Apportionment Study
candidates.authors: Li, Bo; Hu, Caiping; Liu, Zhizheng; Gao, Shuai; Wei, Ziqi; Wei, Yue …
candidates._abstract: Karst groundwater is the principal water supply for Zaozhuang City and an essential safeguard for the local environment. In May 2025, 131 karst groundwater samples were collected and analysed using Piper, Durov, and Gibbs diagrams; ion ratios; mineral saturation indices; and multivariate statistics, and the sources of the dissolved constituents were quantified with positive matrix factorisation (PMF). The water is weakly alkaline, with pH between 7.04 and 7.78 (mean 7.33) and total dissolved solids (TDSs) between 288 and 2578 mg/L (mean 609.10 mg/L). HCO3− and Ca2+ are the dominant ions, and the water is mainly of the HCO3−Ca type. Rock weathering and mineral dissolution, together with anthropogenic inputs, control the water chemistry: Ca2+, Mg2+ and HCO3− are derived mainly from carbonate weathering and dissolution, SO42− from the dissolution of sulfate minerals such as gypsum, Na+, K+ and Cl− from evaporite dissolution and anthropogenic inputs, and NO3− mainly from agricultural activities; cation exchange modifies the ionic balance but does not add solute mass. The PMF model resolves four sources—carbonate weathering, agricultural nitrogen input, sulfate mineral dissolution, and halite dissolution together with anthropogenic salt input—which account for 36.85%, 27.41%, 24.81% and 10.92% of the solute mass, respectively. Carbonate weathering supplies most of the HCO3− and Mg2+, the agricultural nitrogen factor accounts for 95.62% of the NO3−, sulfate mineral dissolution for 83.92% of the SO42−, and the halite–anthropogenic salt factor for 71.32% of the Na+ and 43.89% of the Cl−. Mineral dissolution and water–rock interaction are the main sources of the solutes, while agricultural nitrogen and salt input are the principal anthropogenic contributions. Carbonate and sulfate mineral dissolution together carry about 62% of the solute mass and agricultural nitrogen and salt input about 38%, so the protection of this aquifer should focus on nitrate from farming and salt and sulfate inputs in the urban and mining districts.

candidates.title: Sources, Transformation, and Fate of Groundwater Nitrate Under Intensive Anthropogenic Pressures in the Lower Yellow River Basin: Insights From Hydrochemistry and Multi‐Isotope Analysis
candidates.authors: Yan, Shi; Zhang, Tianxiang; Yan, Zigang; Wang, Shuai; Cheng, Xiaoman; Zhang, Yali …
candidates._abstract: ABSTRACT Enhanced human activities have increased nitrate contamination in groundwater, threatening water‐supply safety and public health. This study examined nitrate sources and transformation processes in 29 shallow groundwater samples from the lower Yellow River Basin, a region subject to intensive agricultural, industrial, and domestic pressures. The observed NO 3 − ‐N concentrations ranged from 0.37 to 177.95 mg/L. Self‐organizing maps, the MixSIAR model, and hydrochemical and multi‐isotope analyses identified five hydrochemical clusters. Across all samples, the mean proportional contributions of soil nitrogen and chemical fertilizers were 52.6% and 31.0%, respectively, indicating that these two sources dominated groundwater nitrate. Sewage/manure and industrial or mining wastewater made smaller overall contributions, but their relative importance increased in areas affected by stronger human activities. The isotope and hydrochemical evidence indicated that nitrification was a key process increasing groundwater nitrate concentrations; this effect was particularly pronounced in the northwestern groundwater convergence zone, where soil nitrogen accumulation was relatively high. These findings suggest that anthropogenic inputs not only introduce nitrate directly but also enhance the leaching and transformation of soil‐ and fertilizer‐derived nitrogen. The results support targeted groundwater management through precision fertilization, soil nitrogen monitoring, wastewater control, and priority protection of vulnerable recharge and convergence areas.

candidates.title: A century of streamwater quality degradation by input from urban water infrastructure as revealed by tree-ring records
candidates.authors: Sananda, Josiah M.; Banner, Jay L.; Nachimuthu, Sneha; Black, Bryan A.; Abella-Gutiérrez, J. L.; Faust, Kasey M. …
candidates._abstract: Abstract The transfer of water from urban water networks to natural streams is a driver of streamwater quality degradation that likely occurs worldwide. We develop a new proxy using tree-ring strontium isotope ratios ( 87 Sr/ 86 Sr) to reconstruct multidecadal histories of municipal-water contributions to natural streams. We apply this approach to three watersheds spanning highly urbanized, rapidly urbanizing, and rural conditions in central Texas, USA. Municipal water has persistently dominated streamflow (>90%) in the urban watershed since at least 1945, only 25 years after the initial expansion of Austin’s municipal water infrastructure network. In the rapidly urbanizing watershed, the modeled municipal-water component of stream baseflow increased from approximately 12% to 33% over only 35 years- a 175% increase that coincided with an 85% increase in population density. In contrast, municipal-water contributions have remained low in the rural watershed since the 1840s. The timing of Sr isotope increases in the urban and rapidly urbanizing watersheds indicates that municipal-water contributions can substantially alter stream chemistry within just two decades of water infrastructure installation. This proxy allows the reconstruction of water-quality degradation over periods of urban growth in the 20th and 21st centuries, including periods that predate the initiation of modern water-quality monitoring. Our approach provides a tool for diagnosing the resilience of water infrastructure under accelerating urban growth and climate stress, informing proactive strategies to protect freshwater resources worldwide.

candidates.title: Drivers of Dissolved Thorium Isotope Distributions Along the Adélie Land Margin, East Antarctica: The Roles of Reversible Scavenging, Conservative Transport, and Lithogenic Supply
candidates.authors: Williams, Thomas J.; Davies, Andrea M. L.; Latour, Pauline Marie Aurelie; Rowland, G; Chase, ﻿Zanna; Noble, Taryn L. …
candidates._abstract: Abstract In this study, we present a mix of full‐depth profiles and near‐bottom observations of dissolved 230 Th and 232 Th from the Adélie Land margin in East Antarctica, a key site of Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) formation. We show that the distribution of dissolved Th isotopes in this region is governed by a combination of reversible scavenging, conservative transport and strong lithogenic inputs, especially on the continental shelf. A model incorporating both reversible scavenging and the upwelling of Circumpolar Deep Water successfully reproduces observed 230 Th xs distributions in the upper and mid‐water column. However, deviations at depth point to additional processes, such as enhanced scavenging near the seafloor, and inputs of 232 Th from benthic and/or suspended sediment dissolution. Exceptionally high inputs of 232 Th to bottom waters on the Adélie shelf, likely sourced from glaciogenic sediments near the Mertz Glacier, are observed. This lithogenic inputs impart a distinct elevated 232 Th/ 230 Th xs signature to shelf waters, which appears to be largely removed via scavenging before entering the abyssal ocean within the AABW. In contrast, the upper 200 m of the water column shows offshore transport of shelf‐derived 232 Th within Winter Water (WW). Based on the strong correlation between 232 Th/ 230 Th xs and dissolved manganese (dMn) in Shelf Water samples, we estimate ∼75% of the dMn observed in WW is sourced from the dissolution of shelf sediment. As WW is progressively mixed into overlying surface waters, this source likely acts as a “slow release” pathway of dMn to the euphotic zone, potentially supporting biological productivity.

candidates.title: Macrofauna Associated With Submarine Groundwater Discharge Sites and a Cold Seep in Svalbard Fjords
candidates.authors: Schramm, Johanna; Hong, Wei‐Li; Hietbrink, Sophie ten; Szymczycha, Beata; Knies, Jochen Manfred; Sen, Arunima
candidates._abstract: Submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) is the flow of subsurface water into the ocean. To assess its impact on the Svalbard benthos, the composition of macrobenthos was investigated in relation to sediment physico-chemical conditions. SGD has been seen to generate seep-like ecosystems in subarctic locations through the transport of reduced chemicals such as methane. Therefore, we compared the benthos of three Svalbard fjord SGD locations to a Svalbard shelf seep location. However, contrary to our expectations, the SGD locations did not resemble the sampled cold seep. Methane was not detectable in sediment porewater, free sulfide concentrations were low, and diversity and abundance were extremely low, despite shallow water depths (40-117 m). It is possible that the combination of freshwater stress, limited chemosynthetic primary production, and high glacimarine sedimentation rates typical of glacier-proximal fjord environments together result in an inhospitable environment for many marine benthic taxa at Svalbard fjord SGD locations. As the Arctic warms and glaciers transition from marine- to land-terminating, SGD fluxes may change and the sedimentary overprint on SGD-related ecological effects may diminish. Whether SGD will eventually emerge as an ecologically relevant process in Arctic fjord systems remains an open question, but one that will become increasingly pertinent as permafrost thaws and glaciers continue to retreat.
